Each business's current rating is on the Food Standards Agency website.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Micky Mellon says the Oldham-Rochdale derby is as good as any he has been involved with in football. The neighbouring teams go head to head for the fifth time under the Scot's tenure - the first of which was his first game in charge of Oldham Athletic. Latics came out on top of that seven-goal thriller, on October 21, 2023. And Mellon said it was on that occasion that he got a real sense of what the fixture means to both clubs and both sets of supporters. More: Oldham Athletic aim to extend 10-year unbeaten league run against rivals Rochdale More: Micky Mellon's football focus wish for derby day after penalty award proves incorrect "I'll be honest with you it wasn't one I was aware of before I came here. I know the proximity was close but I was never really in this area to be involved in that," he explained. "But I was soon shown that it was a big game in the build-up to it when I first came here, and it being my first game as manager, I definitely saw that it had a lovely bit of spice about it. And I mean that in the nicest sense because I want it to be all about football. It had a lovely bit of competition about it that I thought was special and I'm really looking forward to going and taking part in that game again.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Resilient Roch is an innovative flood and climate resilience programme delivered through a partnership between Rochdale Borough Council and the National Flood Forum. Funded by the Flood and Coastal Innovation Programme (FCIP), the project seeks to improve resilience among households and communities vulnerable to flooding, particularly in disadvantaged and diverse neighbourhoods. Resilient Roch is an innovative flood and climate resilience programme delivered through a partnership between Rochdale Borough Council and the National Flood Forum. Funded by the Flood and Coastal Innovation Programme (FCIP), the project seeks to improve resilience among households and communities vulnerable to flooding, particularly in disadvantaged and diverse neighbourhoods. Rather than relying on conventional consultation methods, Resilient Roch adopts a relationship-first approach that builds trust through long-term engagement with residents, community organisations, schools and local stakeholders. By integrating flood resilience with wider issues such as housing, health, wellbeing and climate awareness, the programme strengthens community preparedness and adaptation. Rochdale has a long history of flooding, including major events such as the 2015 Storm Eva floods, which affected hundreds of homes and businesses and exposed wider social vulnerabilities. Research highlighted that flood risk disproportionately affects disadvantaged communities, particularly where poor housing, low incomes, limited insurance uptake and institutional distrust intersect. Traditional engagement and consultation approaches often struggle to reach those most vulnerable to flooding, including marginalised communities, non-English speakers and socially isolated residents. The project aimed to increase flood and climate resilience across vulnerable communities while addressing barriers that limit participation. Key objectives included improving flood literacy, supporting the uptake of property flood resilience measures, strengthening financial resilience through insurance awareness, encouraging community ownership of flood preparedness and increasing understanding of climate risks. The programme also sought to develop stronger partnerships between residents, community organisations, local authorities and other stakeholders to create lasting resilience and community capacity. Resilient Roch adopted a place-based, relationship-led model of engagement that prioritised trust, local knowledge and long-term community presence. The project built on more than a decade of collaboration between Rochdale Borough Council and the National Flood Forum (NFF), enabling the programme to draw on established community trust, local knowledge and existing relationships rather than starting engagement from scratch.

candidates.source_title: MP Welcomes New Young Futures Hub For Rochdale - Rochdale Times
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Rochdale will receive a new Young Futures Hub, bringing together support and opportunities for young people in the local community. The new hub will bring together mental health support, employment and skills opportunities, sport, creative activities and crime prevention services. Rochdale Council will also receive support through the Local Youth Transformation programme to strengthen leadership, train its workforce and build lasting local partnerships. The new Young Futures Hub will provide young people in Rochdale aged 10 to 18 — and up to 25 for those with SEND — with access to seamless, holistic support. Alongside open-access sport, creative activities and trusted youth workers, the hub will connect young people with mental health support, skills and training, routes into employment and crime prevention services. The expansion forms part of the Government’s National Youth Strategy, Youth Matters, launched by Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy in December, 2025, and co-produced with 14,000 young people through the State of the Nation survey. The survey highlighted that many young people have been left without access to safe, supportive environments or a community to belong to, while reliance on online interaction has grown in the absence of face-to-face opportunities. candidates.source_title: Rochdale's magical Ignite Fire Festival returns this November with brand new displays - inyourarea.co.uk
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Spectacular fire sculptures, lights and music will transform Rochdale Town Hall square this November A spectacular family festival will transform the square and gardens around Rochdale Town Hall this autumn. The Ignite Fire Festival is returning to the borough for three evenings of magical entertainment, complete with brand-new trails and attractions. Organised by Rochdale Development Agency, the free night-time event promises magical and immersive trails of fire, lights, and sound across Broadfield Slopes and the newly restored town hall grounds. The event runs from Friday, November 20 to Sunday, November 22, 2026, with the borough's official Christmas lights switch-on taking place on the Sunday evening. Last year, more than 10,000 people attended the festivities. Visitors will be able to walk through fiery displays, blazing sculptures, and an incredible illuminated installation created by multi-award-winning outdoor arts specialists Walk the Plank. Community arts will also take centre stage, with a performance called 'Fireflies' featuring as part of the Culture Co-op programme. The showcase brings together Rochdale’s Skylight Circus Arts, interactive arts group Travelling Light Circus, and local residents who have trained specially to perform mesmerising fire-spinning feats. Councillor Sue Smith, cabinet member for communities and co-operation at Rochdale Borough Council, said: “Ignite Fire Festival has been a huge hit with audiences across Greater Manchester and in just three years has grown to become one of the most popular events in the borough. This year, there will be really exciting new elements and attractions that will surprise, educate and entertain the whole family. Get the dates in your diary and look forward to the ultimate winter experience, and the perfect build-up to our Christmas lights switch-on.” The festival is funded by Rochdale Borough Council, Greater Manchester Combined Authority's Flexible Fund, and Rochdale Development Agency, in partnership with Walk the Plank and Culture Co-op. candidates.source_summary: Delivering for Rochdale, from our streets to the world stage inyourarea.co.uk
candidates.source_title: Delivering for Rochdale, from our streets to the world stage - inyourarea.co.uk
candidates.source_body_excerpt: When I was a lad growing up on a council estate in Spotland, the idea that a Rochdale MP might one day sit round a table in government would have seemed far-fetched. For nearly two hundred years this town sent its members to Parliament without a single one of them holding a departmental ministerial post. That changed this summer, and I still feel the weight of it. Being appointed Minister for Early Education by Prime Minister Andy Burnham is the honour of my working life. But a title only matters if it delivers something real for the people back home. So this month I want to tell you what that job has actually meant for Rochdale. Much of my brief is about giving children the best possible start in life, and over the holidays I saw exactly what that looks like on the ground. At KYP, at BACP, at Aspire 2 Inspire in Greenbank, and with the Rochdale Nigerian Community Association in Broadfield Park, I watched local youngsters get a proper meal and a day full of sport, science and fun through the Government's Holiday Activities and Food programme. As the minister now responsible for that programme across the whole country, there is a real pride in seeing our own community groups make it work so well right here. I also visited the Best Start Family Hub on Derby Street in Heywood, one of seventeen hubs across our borough that support families from bump and birth through those crucial early years. That support makes a real difference to families across our borough, and I will fight to expand it. None of this is charity. It is the difference a Government makes when it decides that where you are born should never decide how far you get. That same principle runs through the £20m of Pride in Place money coming to Smallbridge, Hurstead and Belfield over the next ten years. This is your money to shape, so I have been out and about hearing what local people actually want from it, from Haroon's chippy on Stevenson Square to the team at Cohen's Chemist. The whole point of this fund is to give local people a real say, and I intend to make sure that promise is kept. Ministerial red boxes have not kept me away from the things that make our town what it is. Over the past few weeks I have cheered on the Hornets, welcomed the veterans of Get Together After Serving as they opened their brilliant new cafe opposite Rochdale AFC, joined the Armed Forces Breakfast Club at the Flying Horse for Parachute Regiment veteran Brian Lamb's 90th birthday, and stood in a packed Town Hall Square as OMD paid tribute to the town where they began. Rochdale at its very best. This week my work takes me a good deal further afield. I am in Paris representing the United Kingdom at UNESCO's Digital Learning Week, where education ministers from more than twenty-five countries are wrestling with one of the biggest questions of our age: how we make the most of artificial intelligence in our classrooms without losing what makes teaching human.

The three main acting areas encompass a central one that transforms from the Khan family’s kitchen to their business - a fish and chip shop, and briefly to their front parlour; another to represent their back yard, complete with the “shed” that bundle of nervous energy, youngster Sajit retreats to and “sunbathes” on top of in his protective but rather smelly parka. and another, representing the base of a factory chimney, with a balustrade where the brothers can be together, away from mum and dad. candidates.source_body_excerpt: Parking restrictions and traffic calming have been given the green light to make a “dangerous road” in Middleton safer. Last night, Middleton Township Committee approved a traffic order which will introduce three pedestrian crossing islands, extend bus stops, reduce on-street parking and narrow parts of Grimshaw Lane following problems with speeding, serious crashes, including a fatality, and inconsiderate parking blocking buses. The scheme was called in to be considered by the committee following objections from 11 residents, with the main concern being the loss of parking outside homes. After the meeting, Cllr Dylan Williams, ward councillor and Rochdale Council portfolio holder for highways and facilities, shared: “It has taken four-and-a-half years to get to this point. The road is very dangerous. There have been multiple RTAs, parked cars crashed into, property damaged repeatedly and a fatality. “The road layout was identified as a major factor in the number of accidents and this scheme addresses this. “The islands narrow the road and force the cars to slow down. The narrowing of junctions with disabled access crossings include Shawbury Street, Sedgley Street and the two Sandy Lanes. “We carried out extensive consultation on this scheme. Apart from the 11 objectors, everyone we spoke to was very supportive. “The meeting became very heated with some of the objectors who attended. The main point of contention was parking.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: State Comptroller Tom DiNapoli, inset, has agreed to start an audit of Rochdale Village, after a carrying charge spike last year. The New York State Comptroller’s Office says it is planning on starting an audit of the finances of Rochdale Village, at the urging of local elected officials. “I am writing to let you know that we have formally engaged the audit of Roachdale Village Inc.’s finances,” wrote Comptroller Tom DiNapoli in a letter dated Aug. 25 and addressed to the city councilman, Ty Hankerson (D-Jamaica), as well as the area’s state reps: Assemblymembers Vivian Cook (D-Jamaica) and Khaleel Anderson (D-South Ozone Park), and Sens. Leroy Comrie (D-St. Albans) and James Sanders Jr. (D-South Ozone Park). Hankerson posted the letter on his Instagram page on Sept. 8 and wrote, in the caption, “ROCHDALE, I’ve got good news! The audit is coming and DHCR has officially been engaged for the reassessment of carrying charges,” he wrote, in reference to the Division of Housing and Community Renewal, the state agency that oversees the financially troubled Mitchell-Lama co-op, home to 25,000 people, and hit with $17.7 million in past-due water bills, along with interest. “We’ve been working really, really hard on this,” Hankerson told the Chronicle in an interview. In early August, Hankerson penned a letter addressed to DiNapoli requesting “a full audit” of the co-op’s finances, and a recalculation of the carrying charges that its members are paying in lieu of rent. “Residents should not be asked to carry costs that have not been fully reviewed, explained, and justified,” Hankerson wrote at the time. Last year, the DHCR increased carrying charges at the complex by more than 20 percent, leading to protests.

candidates.source_summary: A hat trick of announcements has cemented Middleton’s renewed regeneration drive, as its Mayoral Development Corporation continues to take shape.
candidates.source_title: Hat trick of announcements as Middleton’s regeneration moves up a gear – Rochdale Borough Council
candidates.source_body_excerpt: A hat trick of announcements has cemented Middleton’s renewed regeneration drive, as its Mayoral Development Corporation continues to take shape. Among them is news that the Middleton Old Grammar School, recently bought by the council, is expected to announce a new tenant before the end of the year. Founded in 1582, the building in Boarshaw Road aimed to provide free education to children in the parish of Middleton. More recently, it was used as a wedding and events venue before the council took the opportunity to buy the heritage asset when it went up for sale. A feasibility study is now on going, with a view to the building being repaired, refurbished and reopened for community use in the future. The news was announced at an event at Middleton Arena to update residents and businesses about the results of an engagement exercise titled, ‘Our Town, Our Future’ and on going work to create a Mayoral Development Corporation to further drive regeneration in the town. Chaired by the proposed chairs of Middleton’s MDC, Steve Coogan and Rose Marley, and attended by Mayor of Greater Manchester, Bev Craig, and Rochdale Borough Council leader, Councillor Neil Emmott, the event attracted more than 500 residents and local business leaders. The announcements followed news that the council is in the process of acquiring long derelict Warwick Mill and neighbouring 1960s office block, London House, with a view to bringing the mill back into use, possibly as new homes, and demolishing London House. In a further boost, attendees also learned that the Middleton Scout Hut will be repurposed as a community venue, with a full programme of activities and training opportunities for young people. The council owned venue on Long Street has been vacant for 13 years and the council has now agreed a long-term lease with charitable organisation, the Groundwork Trust. Proposals for the building include the creation of a hub for workshops to teach ecology and construction skills. The building will also serve as a base for local environmental projects, and, while opportunities for young people will be a key focus, it will also be a space for community groups to get together to help tackle social isolation.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: Residents have launched a petition to replace a popular kick pitch which is being turned into a car park. The pitch is one of three on the estate. It is managed by the Burnside Centre and is being turned into a car park for the centre following planning permission for change of use. Instead, they are calling for a new pitch to be created on land next to the original. Launching the petition on Change.org, Kelly Burton shared: “For countless children and teenagers in the Burnside Crescent area, the kick pitch behind the old site was more than just a recreational space — it was a community hub where friendships were formed and cherished memories were built. “Every day, hundreds of young players gathered there, practicing their football skills, learning the value of teamwork, and enjoying the joy of outdoor play. “Recently, the kick pitch was removed without prior notice to the public. This decision has left a significant void in our community, with children now deprived of a convenient, safe, and free space to play.

candidates.source_body_excerpt: A haul of fake designer goods worth 'millions' has landed a businessman in court. Assum Malik pleaded guilty to possession of counterfeit goods with intent to supply after more than £2.4 million in fake merchandise was uncovered at a business in Rochdale on January 28, 2022. Malik, of High Elm Road in Hale Barns, initially pleaded not guilty but changed his plea during a hearing at Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court on Monday (September 14). The court heard he was pleading guilty on the basis that he disputed the total value of the goods, but the court heard that Rochdale Council did not accept his lower estimate. Defending, Richard Orme argued there was a significant difference between the council’s valuation and Malik’s, claiming the true figure was closer to half of the stated value. Minshull Street Crown Court (Image: Google Maps) He told the court that Malik had purchased a "job lot" of counterfeit stock for £6,000 and planned to sell it for 'like £20,000'. However, His Honour Judge Jason Macadam said that the £2.4 million value was representative of what the brands would have lost had customers bought counterfeit goods instead of their legitimate ones.

candidates.source_summary: Artists from Rochdale and Kenya have created a 15-metre-high wildlife mural on Brook House in Middleton town centre.
candidates.source_title: Wildlife mural created in Middleton as part of Kenya arts exchange - rochvalleyradio.com
candidates.source_body_excerpt:
The artwork on Oldham Road is part of an international exchange project focusing on endangered species and ecosystems.

The mural has been created through the Endangered Exchange project by Rochdale artist AYLO, also known as Hayley Garner, and Victoria Firth, founder of The Wild Mural Project.

They have been working with local artist Jamie Buckley and Kenyan artist Ninah Tanya as part of the project.

The artwork measures around 15 metres high and 10 metres wide.

It features a hen harrier, large heath butterfly, emperor dragonfly, sphagnum moss and wildfires.

The words "Save our tomorrow today" also appear in Swahili, while the design includes Kanga fabric associated with Kenyan culture.

The project has been developed in partnership with Lancashire Wildlife Trust.

Hayley Garner said: "Victoria and I came up with the idea of 'Endangered Exchange' - an international collaboration that could create vibrant community driven art that inspires a deeper connection between people and the planet.

"It's not just painting, it's about developing artists and giving opportunities they might never otherwise have had, connecting communities across the world and showing how creativity can bring people together."

Ninah Tanya travelled from Nairobi to Middleton for a two-week artist residency after spending the past year being mentored by Victoria Firth in Kenya.

She said: "This is the biggest mural I've worked on and it has been an amazing experience. I've visited Rochdale too to see the murals there, painted by artists I admire, and the town hall is beautiful."

Jamie Buckley is due to travel to Kenya next month for the second part of the exchange.

He will work with the other artists and local communities on workshops, wildlife research and a second mural focusing on Kenya's natural environment.

Victoria Firth said: "We only have one planet to live on, so we need to take care of it. I think this new Middleton mural shares a powerful message about our climate, and species that will disappear, as well as creating a connection between Middleton and Kenya."

Councillor Sue Smith, cabinet member for communities and co-operation at Rochdale Borough Council, said the project followed feedback from residents through the Middleton Co-operating "Our Town, Our Future" engagement.

She said: "This striking new mural is a powerful reminder that climate change is one of the greatest challenges facing our planet and the wildlife that depends on it."

The project is being recorded for a documentary covering the artists' journeys, mentoring and cultural exchange.

The UK stage forms part of the Rochdale Creates cultural programme and is part-funded by The Butterfly Effected CIC, Rochdale Development Agency and Rochdale Borough Council.

The Kenyan stage is being supported by The Wild Mural Projects, Caparol Paints Kenya and Turtle Bay Beach Club in Watamu.

candidates.source_summary: Plans to turn a former Conservative club and bowling green into a modern wedding and events venue have been refused after the benefits of the scheme were outweighed by the harm it could cause
candidates.source_title: Wedding venue plan refused over ‘harm’ development could cause - Rochdale Times
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Plans to turn a former Conservative club and bowling green into a modern wedding and events venue have been refused after the benefits of the scheme were outweighed by the harm it could cause. Mr M Suleman appealed to the Planning Inspectorate about the length of time Rochdale Council took to consider his application to turn the former Middleton Conservative Club and Kohinoor Banqueting Hall into a new multi-functional events space in Long Street. Plans submitted in February included a part single/part two-storey side extension, external stairway and retaining wall, creation of access to rear and conversion of a former bowling green into a parking area. The appeal was launched while the council considered issues including pedestrian access and safe routes to the proposed wedding venue; the impact of noise on nearby residents, including the first-floor flat within the building which may be used by a caretaker; air quality; and concerns about protected species that might be affected by the development. Planning inspector Roger Catchpole said: “The council failed to give notice within the statutory time period but has set out its putative reasons for refusal. “I find the main issues to be the effect of the proposal on the character and appearance of the area, bearing in mind the special attention that should be paid to the desirability of preserving the special interest of the adjacent Grade II* listed building, known as Long Street Methodist Church, Long Street Methodist Sunday School and the extent to which it would preserve or enhance the character or appearance of the Middleton Town Centre Conservation Area.” Mr Catchpole agreed with the council that the plans, including the extension, were “generally appropriate in terms of the established street scene” and that it was set back from important historic elements of Long Street. “However, I cannot rule out direct harm to the fabric of the listed building given the proximity of the ramp and the lack of detail concerning its construction,” he said.

candidates.source_summary: Artists from Rochdale and Kenya have brought a huge new endangered wildlife themed mural to Brook House in Middleton.
candidates.source_title: International exchange: Middleton goes wild for nature inspired mural – Rochdale Borough Council
candidates.source_body_excerpt: Drivers and pedestrians in Middleton town centre are noticing some new wildlife popping up along their commute. Artists from Rochdale and Samburu, Kenya have brought a huge new endangered wildlife themed mural to Brook House on Oldham Road, encouraging residents to understand the importance of ecosystems as well as the conservation efforts that enhance wildlife and protect the planet. Lead artists - AYLO (Hayley Garner) from Rochdale and Kenyan based Victoria Firth, founder of global arts initiative The Wild Mural Project have been mentoring local artist Jamie Buckley and Kenyan based Ninah Tanya, to create their first international masterpiece in Middleton. Hayley, curator of the Common Walls International Mural Festival that has transformed public spaces with large-scale artwork in Rochdale said: "Victoria and I came up with the idea of 'Endangered Exchange' - an international collaboration that could create vibrant community driven art that inspires a deeper connection between people and the planet. It's not just painting, it's about developing artists and giving opportunities they might never otherwise have had, connecting communities across the world and showing how creativity can bring people together." A large heath butterfly - classed as endangered in the UK features in the artwork. Developed in partnership with the Lancashire Wildlife Trust, the Endangered Exchange initiative follows 'The Herds', the groundbreaking public art project that visited Heywood last year as part of Manchester International Festival and Rochdale's year as Greater Manchester Town of Culture, encouraging communities to renew their bond with the natural world. The striking 15 metre high x 10 metre wide mural features species that tell an interconnected story: a Hen Harrier, large heath butterfly - classed as endangered in the UK, emperor dragon fly, sphagnum moss that holds water and allows peat to form, and wildfires. Referencing the projects connection to Keyna, the phrase 'Save our tomorrow today' is written in Swahili - a call to notice what is around us, understand how connected it all is and to protect these landscapes before the warning becomes a loss we cannot reverse. The new mural has been designed to represent mounting pressure being placed on landscapes that may appear strong but are held together by delicate relationships between water, plants, insects, birds and climate. The artwork also features Kanga, a striking fabric that reflects the rich culture of Keyna.
